en: The Sūtra on the Merit of Bathing the Buddha, translated by the Da Tang Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (Yìjìng).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as an immeasurable and boundless multitude of great bodhisattvas, along with the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others, all of whom had gathered like clouds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati was seated among the assembly. Out of compassion for all sentient beings, he reflected thus:
"By what causes and conditions do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, attain a pure body, complete with the primary and secondary marks?"
Again, he thought:
"If all classes of sentient beings were to encounter a Tathāgata, draw near to him, and make offerings to him, the merit and reward they would obtain would be immeasurable and boundless."

I do not yet know, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, what kind of offerings all sentient beings should make and what merit they should cultivate, so that their roots of goodness may swiftly reach the ultimate state of unsurpassed bodhi.
Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask a question; I pray that you will deign to grant me your hearing.
The Buddha said, "Good son!
"I shall explain it for you according to your questions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions do the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas attain a pure body, fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks?"
Furthermore, all sentient beings who encounter a Tathāgata, draw near to him, and make offerings to him, obtain blessings and rewards that are immeasurable and boundless.

I do not yet know what kind of offerings all sentient beings should make, nor what merit they should cultivate after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, so that their roots of goodness may swiftly reach the ultimate state of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You are able to pose such a question for the sake of those sentient beings of the future."
"Listen attentively now, reflect upon it well, and practice according to what is taught!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying:

“Good son! You should know that because giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the powers, the fearlessnesses, all Buddha-dharmas, and the knowledge of all modes are perfectly pure, the Tathāgata is pure.”

If one makes various offerings with a pure mind to such Buddhas and Tathāgatas—arranging incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, canopies, and mats before them; adorning them with various ornaments; bathing their venerable forms with exquisite fragrant water; and burning incense that universally perfumes the Dharma-realm while directing the mind toward it.

Furthermore, by means of food and drink, drums and music, stringed songs, and hymns of praise for the Tathāgata’s unique qualities (āveṇika-guṇa), they make supreme vows and dedicate [the merit] toward the unsurpassed ocean of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā). The merit thus produced is immeasurable and boundless, continuing uninterruptedly until the attainment of Bodhi.
Why is this? Because the merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata are inconceivable, innumerable, and peerless.
O son of good family!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess three bodies, namely: the Dharma-body, the Enjoyment-body, and the Transformation-body.
After my parinirvāṇa, if you wish to make offerings to these three bodies, you should make offerings to the śarīras.
However, there are two kinds:
first, the bodily bone śarīra;
second, the dharma-verse śarīra.
He then spoke in verse:
"All phenomena arise from conditions; The Tathāgata has explained their cause.
The cessation of those phenomena through the exhaustion of their causes— This is what the Great Śramaṇa teaches."
"Whether it be men, women, or the fivefold assembly of bhikṣus, you should fashion images of the Buddha.

If one lacks the means, one may fashion even something as small as a grain of barley; a stūpa the size of a jujube fruit, with a banner-pole like a needle, a parasol like a grain of flour, and śarīra-relics like mustard seeds, or else inscribe dharma verses within it."
With such rare and precious offerings as these, one should, according to one's own capacity, with utmost sincerity and reverence, act in a manner no different from my manifesting in person.
“Good son! If there are sentient beings who can perform such supreme offerings, they will accomplish fifteen kinds of extraordinary merits with which to adorn themselves:
first, they will always possess a sense of shame and remorse;”
Second, to give rise to pure faith;
third, for the mind to be upright and sincere;
fourth, to draw near to virtuous friends.
Fifth, entering untainted wisdom;
sixth, constantly beholding all Buddhas;
seventh, perpetually upholding the True Dharma.
Eighth, they are able to practice according to what they have taught;
ninth, they will be born at will in pure Buddha-lands;
tenth, if they are born among humans, they will be of noble lineage and high status, honored and revered by others, giving rise to a heart of joy.
Eleventh, being born among human beings, they naturally recollect the Buddha;
twelfth, the hosts of māras cannot harm or afflict them;
thirteenth, they are able to protect and uphold the True Dharma in the final age.
"Fourteenth, they shall be protected by the empowerment of all Buddhas of the ten directions;
fifteenth, they shall swiftly achieve the accomplishment of the fivefold Dharma-body.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"After my parinirvāṇa, those who are able to make offerings to the śarīra,
or construct stūpas and images of the Tathāgata,
and at those sites of images and stūpas, smear and cleanse maṇḍalas— "
With various kinds of incense and flowers, scatter them upon it;
with pure and wondrous scented water, bathe the body of the image;
and with foods and drinks of the finest flavors, offer them all as an act of worship.
Praising the virtues of the Tathāgata, Immeasurable and inconceivable—
His skillful means, wisdom, and supernormal powers, He swiftly reaches the further shore,
Attaining the adamantine body, Endowed with the thirty-two marks.
With the eighty secondary marks, he delivers all living beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom, having heard these verses, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should future sentient beings bathe the image?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying:
"You all should give rise to a mind of right mindfulness toward the Tathāgata; do not cling to the two extremes and become confused regarding emptiness and existence;
and regarding all categories of wholesome qualities, remain thirsting for them without weariness."
One should skillfully cultivate wisdom through the three gates of liberation;
constantly seek transcendence and do not dwell in birth and death;
and give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, vowing to swiftly accomplish the three bodies.

“Good son! I have already taught you the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Pāramitās. Now, for your sake and for that of all kings, princes, ministers, ladies of the inner court, devas, nāgas, humans, and spirits, I shall further explain the ritual for bathing the image. This is the foremost among all offerings, surpassing the gift of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”

When bathing the image, one should grind ox-head sandalwood, white sandalwood, red sandalwood, aloeswood, frankincense, saffron, camphor, zerumbet, and patchouli upon a clean stone to create fragrant paste; this should then be used as scented water and placed in a pure vessel.

In a clean place, construct an altar using fine earth, either square or circular, according to its size at the time; place a bathing bed upon it, install a Buddha image in the center, bathe it with fragrant water, wash and cleanse it thoroughly, and then pour pure water over it again.
All water used must be filtered thoroughly to ensure that no insects are harmed.

When using water for bathing an image, one should take it up with two fingers and place it upon one’s own crown; this is called "Auspicious Water" (śrīvāri). It should be poured onto clean ground and not stepped upon with the feet.
Wipe the image clean with a fine, soft cloth, burn various famous incenses until the fragrance permeates everywhere, and then install it in its original place. "Good son!
By performing such bathing of the Buddha images, you and this great assembly of humans and devas shall presently enjoy wealth and happiness, be free from illness, and live long lives;
whatever you seek and pray for shall be fulfilled according to your wishes;
and all your friends, relatives, and kinsmen shall be entirely secure and at peace.
May they forever bid farewell to the eight difficulties and emerge eternally from the source of suffering;
may they no longer receive a female body and swiftly attain perfect enlightenment.
Having thus made this dedication, he further burned various incenses and, before the image, joined his palms with sincere devotion and spoke these words of praise:
"I now bathe all the Tathāgatas, The assembly adorned with the merit of pure wisdom;
May the multitudes of sentient beings in the five turbidities Swiftly realize the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata."
The fragrance of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision pervades the lands of the ten directions, ever fragrant;
may this incense smoke likewise act as a Buddha-work, immeasurable and boundless.
I also pray that the wheel of suffering in the three realms may cease, That all may be freed from feverish heat and attain cool serenity,
That all may give rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta, And forever emerge from the river of craving to reach the other shore.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, at that time there were immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas within the assembly who attained the stainless samādhi;
immeasurable devas attained non-retrogressive wisdom;
and the assembly of śrāvakas made vows to seek the fruit of Buddhahood.
Eighty-four thousand sentient beings all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
We are fortunate to have received the Great Master’s compassionate pity and his instruction on the ritual for bathing the image.

We now exhort kings, ministers, and all those with faith who delight in merit to bathe the venerable form every day; thereby they shall obtain great benefit. May you always receive this upon the crown of your head and joyfully practice it!
The Sutra on the Merit of Bathing the Buddha (Yufoshengongde jing)
